subChunks.title: Code Smells & Extract Method
subChunks.hookHtml: Code that works is not the same as code that is maintainable. Refactoring is the discipline of improving the internal structure of code without changing its external behaviour. It is the craft skill that separates junior engineers from senior ones.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is Refactoring?

Refactoring means changing the code's structure — names, method boundaries, class organisation — without changing what the code does. The behaviour is preserved; the design improves. Refactoring always needs tests to verify nothing broke.

Common Code Smells

  • Long Method: a method that does too much. Split into smaller, named methods.
  • Magic Numbers/Strings: unexplained literal values. Extract to named constants.
  • Duplicate Code: the same logic in two places. Extract to a shared method.
  • Dead Code: variables, methods, or imports that are never used. Delete them.
  • God Class: a class that knows too much and does too much. Split by responsibility.
  • Deeply Nested Conditionals: if inside if inside if. Use guard clauses or extract methods.
  • Feature Envy: a method that uses another class's data more than its own. Move the method there.

Extract Method

The most-used refactoring: pull a block of code out of a method into its own named method.

// BEFORE — long method doing everything
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    // validate
    if (order == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("null order");
    if (order.getItems().isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("empty order");
    // calculate total
    double total = 0;
    for (Item item : order.getItems()) total += item.getPrice() * item.getQuantity();
    // apply discount
    if (order.getMembership() == GOLD) total *= 0.9;
    // print receipt
    System.out.println("Total: " + total);
}

// AFTER — each concern in its own method
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    validate(order);
    double total = calculateTotal(order);
    total = applyDiscount(order, total);
    printReceipt(total);
}

private void validate(Order order) { ... }
private double calculateTotal(Order order) { ... }
private double applyDiscount(Order order, double total) { ... }
private void printReceipt(double total) { ... }

Replace Magic Numbers

// BEFORE
if (total > 1000) total *= 0.85;

// AFTER
static final double PREMIUM_THRESHOLD = 1000.0;
static final double PREMIUM_DISCOUNT = 0.85;
if (total > PREMIUM_THRESHOLD) total *= PREMIUM_DISCOUNT;

storyBeats.text: The Academy's code review chamber has a wall of scrolls. Red marks cover one scroll in particular — not because it's wrong, but because no one can read it fast enough to know if it's right.

storyBeats.speaker: Senior Enchanter Dev
storyBeats.text: Working code is the minimum bar. Maintainable code is the professional bar. A 200-line method that works is a liability — the next developer will be afraid to touch it, and when a bug hides in line 147, they'll have to read all 200 lines to find it. That fear is the real cost of bad structure.

storyBeats.speaker: Senior Enchanter Dev
storyBeats.text: Code smells are patterns that signal structural problems. A long method. Magic numbers with no explanation. The same logic copy-pasted in three places. Dead code cluttering the class. A class that knows everything about everything. Each smell has a corresponding refactoring to fix it.

storyBeats.speaker: Extract Method before/after
Senior Enchanter Dev
storyBeats.text: The golden rule of refactoring: never refactor without tests. Your test suite is your safety net. If behaviour breaks, the tests tell you immediately. Refactoring without tests is just rearranging unknown territory in the dark.

learningObjectives: Identify at least five code smells in existing code
Apply Extract Method to decompose a long method into smaller, named methods
Replace magic numbers and strings with named constants
Explain why refactoring requires test coverage before starting
commonMistakes: Refactoring without tests — you cannot verify behaviour is preserved without them
Extracting methods that are still too long — aim for methods that do one thing
Over-extracting trivial one-liners — extracting a single arithmetic expression into a method reduces readability
Renaming poorly without IDE support — missing a usage causes a 'cannot find symbol' error
assessmentCriteria: Can identify at least 5 distinct code smells and name the refactoring that addresses each
Can apply Extract Method to a real 20+ line method and produce at least 3 smaller methods
Can replace magic literals with named constants throughout a class
Can explain what a regression is and why test coverage is a prerequisite for safe refactoring
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain refactoring — what it is, what it is not, and why it matters. Pick one code smell and walk through the refactoring step-by-step. Why do you need tests before you start?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The method below has multiple smells. Refactor it:

  1. Extract a validate() method for the guard clauses
  2. Extract a calcXp() method for the XP calculation
  3. Extract a printResult() method for the output
  4. Replace the magic numbers 3, 50, 100 with named constants
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch, write a well-structured version of: a method processEnrolment(String studentName, int age, String course) that validates (name not blank, age 16-100, course not blank), calculates a fee (base fee 500, +200 if age < 25 for premium support, -50 if course is "ONLINE"), and prints "[name] enrolled in [course] — fee: [fee]". Use at least 3 extracted methods and named constants. Test with Lyria, age 22, course ONLINE.

options: Adding new features without changing existing code
Improving code structure without changing its external behaviour
questions.answer: Improving code structure without changing its external behaviour
questions.explanation: Refactoring is a disciplined technique for restructuring code — renaming, extracting, reorganising — while preserving observable behaviour. The tests should still pass after every refactoring step.

questions.prompt: A developer finds the same 10-line block of code in three different methods. What is the code smell and what is the refactoring?
questions.answer: Duplicate Code — extract the shared block into a single named method and call it from all three places
questions.explanation: Duplicate Code is one of the most common smells. Three copies means three places to update when a bug is found or the logic changes — and three chances to forget one. Extract to a shared method: one place to update, three callers.

questions.prompt: Before refactoring a large class, you realise there are no unit tests for it. What should you do?
options: Proceed anyway — refactoring doesn't change behaviour so tests aren't needed
Write characterisation tests first (capturing current behaviour) then refactor
Rewrite the class from scratch instead of refactoring
Ask a colleague to review the code instead of adding tests
questions.answer: Write characterisation tests first (capturing current behaviour) then refactor
questions.explanation: Characterisation tests (also called golden master tests) lock down the current behaviour by recording inputs and outputs before you start changing anything. Once they pass, you have a safety net. Refactoring without a safety net is how you introduce regressions that only appear in production weeks later.
